history.dynasty: Maurya (Dhavalappadeva/Dhavala, per the 725 CE Dabok stone inscription); the temple's own inscription names the endower as Śivagaṇa; James Tod also recorded a 5th-century inscription of the Jat king Shalinder at Kanswa in 1820
history.period: 738 CE (Vikram Samvat 795) - recorded by an in-situ inscription on the temple wall; extensively rebuilt since
history.summary: The famous 8th-century Kansua Mahadev Shiva temple in Kanswa (Kansua) village, a few kilometres from Kota in Kota district - CSV town 'Kota' is approximate; the temple is at the village of Kansua/Kanswa, now within Kota's industrial outskirts (JK Colony, near Dakaniya Talav railway station). An in-situ Kutila-script inscription dated 738 CE (VS 795) records the temple's construction and endowment by a private individual named Śivagaṇa on the site of the Kaṇvāśrama (ashram of sage Kanva) - the name Kansua derives from Kaṇvāśrama. The inscription mentions ruler Dhavala, likely Dhavalappadeva of the Dabok stone inscription (~725 CE), though he seems to have played no role in the founding. Images of Lakulīśa in prominent positions suggest the temple was once affiliated with the Pāśupata Shaiva sect (Wikipedia/Kanswa). Local legend also attributes the temple to the Pandavas, and some visitor accounts call it an ancient Buddhist site renovated by the Mauryas of Chittor in the 7th century - both weakly sourced, flag as unverified. The temple's signature is the rare four-faced (Chaturmukha) Shiva Lingam, symbolizing Shiva's omnipresence; some sources also claim the linga leans at ~17 degrees (weakly sourced - verify). A sacred tank, Kansua Kund, lies nearby. James Tod found an inscription of the 5th-century Jat king Maharaja Shalinder here in 1820, making Kanswa archaeologically important. Coordinates are from map geocode of Kansua Shiv Mandir.

name: Kansua Temple
town: Kansua (Kanswa) village, Kota (CSV town 'Kota' is approximate - the temple is ~6 km from Kota city in the village of Kansua/Kanswa)
town_description: Kota is a major city on the Chambal River in southeastern Rajasthan, best known nationally as India's coaching-education hub. On the Chambal's banks it also holds a string of old temples - Khade Ganesh Ji, the Mathuradheesh Temple of the old city, and the ancient Kansua Shiv Mandir - set around riverside gardens, the Chambal Garden and the old Patanpole quarter.
tradition: Hinduism (Shaivism; historically associated with Pāśupata Shaiva per Lakulīśa imagery)

travel.railway: Kota Junction is the major railhead; Dakaniya Talav railway station is close to the temple (verify distances).
travel.road: About 6 km from Kota city; at 4VVM+V36, JK Colony, Kota Industrial Area (verify).

visitor_information.best_time: October to March; Maha Shivaratri and Sawan Mondays are the most crowded.
visitor_information.opening_hours: Generally 6:00 AM to 9:00 PM per travel sources (verify - confirm locally). No entry fee; Sunday evening aartis are considered spiritually powerful by local devotees.
